01 / The short version

THE BRANDS ARE
THE ADVANTAGE.

The venues should not all look the same. But every guest should get clear details, working links and an easy next step.

Keep the personality.
Make the next step easy.

MAC has strong brands, real spaces and many reasons to visit. The websites and posts already have useful material. The clearest problems are in the details: old booking dates, wrong link targets, mixed hours and pages that do not agree.

Keep each brand’s style. Give them one shared way to keep facts right and track results. Fix what we can prove first. Then test which posts, ads and pages bring useful requests, bookings and orders.

01 / Fix first

Help guests who are ready.

Fix venue choices, contact links, booking dates and page layout. Check where each button goes before paying to send more guests there.

02 / Connect next

Match the reason for the visit.

Brunch, a night out, tacos and a work event are different choices. Show the right photos, facts, location and next step for each.

03 / Scale with evidence

Count the useful results.

Count finished bookings, useful event requests and orders where the data allows. Views, likes and clicks help explain the story. They are not sales.

What we still need to know

We did not receive ad accounts, website reports, booking records, sales data or the agency contract. We cannot prove ad spend, profit, lost leads or agency value from public pages. The reported agency fee is not used as evidence.

02 / Evidence before opinion

WHAT WE CAN
ACTUALLY PROVE.

Each issue says what we found, why it matters, what to change and how to check the fix. Click a screenshot to make it bigger.

We ranked these by the guest problem, not by guessed lost sales. Work estimates are rough until the website team checks the setup.

03 / Each brand, one by one

ONE PLAYBOOK.
NOT ONE PERSONALITY.

Each brand needs its own reason to visit. Keep the guest’s date, location and goal clear from the first click to the final step.

Shared rules / distinct brands

Share one venue list, link checklist and reporting system. Keep the photos, food stories, events and tone specific to each brand.

Small rules. Big guest questions.

One design. Not one policy.

The published menus have real differences. Keep each venue’s rules close to its booking choice. Staff should confirm them before any page update.

Casa Lola

Six guests, not eight.

The dinner PDF lists an 18% service charge for parties of six or more. Do not copy the other brands’ eight-person rule here.

See dinner menu ›
Cafeteria 15L

Brunch has a time limit.

The brunch menu lists a two-hour dine-in limit. The main menu’s group charge starts at eight guests. Put the relevant rule near the booking step.

See menu ›
Iron Horse

Brunch starts at different times.

The menu lists 9am for R Street and 10am for Folsom, with a 1.5-hour dine-in limit. The main menu’s group charge starts at eight guests.

See menu ›
Mas Taco

Keep the group charge clear.

The booking page and Eats PDF disclose an 18% charge for parties of eight or more. Keep that detail visible as guests pick a location.

See booking page ›

Menus should work well on a phone.

All four dining sites have web dish lists and linked PDF menus. The PDFs we checked carry prices and fuller descriptions. Add those useful details to the web pages too, then keep both versions in sync. Keep the PDFs for printing. This is a suggested improvement, not a claim that the sites are PDF-only.

04 / The guest journey

CHECK THE WHOLE TRIP.
NOT JUST THE PAGE.

Problems often happen when guests move from one place to another: a post to a website, a website to booking, or a form to the events team.

Everyday dining

“Where should we eat?”

  1. DiscoverSearch, Maps, recommendation or a social post
  2. DecideThe right venue, current menu, hours and what the space feels like
  3. ActBook, order, call or get directions without choosing the venue again
  4. ReturnUseful follow-up only when the guest has agreed to receive it

Test: Can a new guest use a phone to find the right place and finish the task? Check the booking result, not just the click.

Nightlife

“What is happening tonight?”

  1. DiscoverAn event date, performer, rooftop photo or local search
  2. DecideDate, time, entry rules and which booking option to choose
  3. ActGuest list, ticket or VIP table with a clear result
  4. ReturnUseful news about future nights, without too many messages

Test: Does the guest know which event is current, what to book and what happens next? Old events should not be the first thing they see.

Private events

“Which space fits our group?”

  1. DiscoverA work planner, celebration, convention or recommendation
  2. DecideEvent type, place, room setup, group size and real examples
  3. ActA useful request sent to the right person with clear next steps
  4. CloseOpen dates, price, deposit or contract, then a confirmed event

Test: Is the venue choice right? Does the request reach the events team? Track time to reply and events booked. Do not promise a reply time staff cannot meet.

MIX / a closer look

Track each way in. Keep the event details the same.

The calendar uses several booking services. That is not a fault by itself. The job is to make each date, price and next step clear.

November 6–8

Guest list + VIP request

The calendar links to SevenRooms for guest list and to MIX’s own VIP form. The November 6 link reached the right Scorpio SZN event at 9:30 PM, with free guest list before 10:30 PM and $15 normal cover.

Check: joining a list is not the same as buying a ticket or booking a table.

November 13 onward

Speakeasy event choices

The November 13 page offers guest list, a paid All Access VIP ticket and separate VIP Tables. Its displayed 9:30 AM start conflicts with MIX’s PM calendar time.

Check: “VIP ticket” and “VIP table” must not look like the same purchase. Confirm full costs and what each includes.

November 14 special event

Separate singles-party tickets

The calendar links the CitySwoon party to its own ticket site and says tickets include the afterparty. We checked the calendar link, not the CitySwoon checkout.

Check: explain whether a special-event ticket also covers regular club entry.

Do not call a deposit the full table price.

The Speakeasy table view lists minimums of $250 for six guests and $350 for ten. It also shows smaller amounts whose role and final totals we did not verify. MIX’s VIP FAQ lists tax plus a 22% service charge. Do not combine these into a guessed total. Ask the venue and booking service to show the full cost and terms clearly before checkout.

Suggested design / not a live booking tool

Start with what the guest needs.

Three simple choices can help guests find the right page without learning the whole group first.

The content we would test

One audience. One occasion. One next step.

These are suggested tests. They are not claims about current ads or promises of better results.

Cafeteria 15L

Show a reason to visit.

Lead with: a real brunch visit or a room being set up for an event.

Show: food arriving, guests in the space and useful venue facts.

Link to: the brunch, table booking or event page that fits the post.

Test: a post about the space versus a post about the food. Compare the same booking goal.

MIX Downtown

Sell this night, not generic nightlife.

Lead with: the actual upcoming date or programming.

Show: rooftop atmosphere, arrival experience and service.

Link to: a dated page with entry and booking information.

Test: a post about this event versus a post about the rooftop. Compare bookings and how often people see each ad.

Iron Horse Tavern

Make location part of the message.

Lead with: a reason to eat at R Street or Folsom.

Show: the actual venue, a signature item and practical access.

Link to: the selected location’s menu and booking flow.

Test: a location-specific post and page versus a general brand post and page.

Mas Taco Bar

Turn craving into a nearby action.

Lead with: a distinctive taco build, group moment or current special.

Show: real preparation and an active venue.

Link to: Arden or R Street, not an ambiguous brand home.

Test: a food post versus a group-night post. Compare orders when those records are available.

Casa Lola

Make the concept easy to choose.

Lead with: a recognizable dining or celebration occasion.

Show: actual space, menu and service experience.

Link to: the matching dining or event path.

Test: an introduction to Casa versus a specific reason to visit.

Café Ami

Give opening news a home.

Lead with: the new concept, then a verified opening milestone.

Show: real menu development, buildout or team story.

Link to: a launch page with honest timing and optional updates.

Test: local signups and first bookings or orders, not views alone.

Unpaid posts: make each one useful

  • Pin the essentials: what the concept is, where it is and how to take the next step.
  • Check profile links, highlights and offers against the same venue list the websites use.
  • Mix food, people, the space, events and useful facts. Choose a posting schedule the team can keep. Use results to guide it.
  • Get permission to use guest and staff photos. Add video captions and easy-to-read text.
  • Look at saves, shares, profile visits and what guests do next. Follower count alone is not the goal.

Paid ads: test before spending more

  • Give dining, nightlife, events and launches separate goals. Each ad should ask for the right next step.
  • Check that links work and results are counted correctly before changing spend.
  • Name ads and links by brand, location, event and version so results are easy to compare.
  • Change one main thing at a time when there is enough traffic to learn. Decide how long to test and what counts as a win.
  • Check how often people see an ad, how they respond and whether it leads to useful results. An old ad is not always a bad ad.
  • Follow age rules and platform policies for alcohol and nightlife ads.
06 / Search, local & reputation

BE EASY TO FIND.
EASIER TO CHOOSE.

Guests search for a specific place. A good-looking website still needs the right hours, phone, menu and booking link.

01 / What guests search for

Answer the useful question.

Make useful pages for real questions: a location, brunch, private dining, group size or a current event. Use search data to decide what to build first.

Done when: each page has a clear title, correct main address, readable menu and working links. Do not copy the same thin page for every location.

02 / Local consistency

Keep every listing current.

Check Google, Apple Maps, Bing, Yelp and booking or order services. Compare each name, address, phone, menu and link with the approved venue list. Plan all changes for the Folsom closure and Café Ami launch.

Done when: one person owns the list, changes are dated, and live pages have been checked. No listing changes have been made as part of this audit.

03 / Reputation

Use reviews to improve the visit.

Read a fair sample of recent reviews for each venue, including praise. Group comments about service, food, value, access and booking. Share repeated problems with the team that can fix them.

Done when: record which reviews were read and who will respond. Do not invent scores, rankings or complaints.

What this does not prove

We did not measure search rank across the area, read all reviews or receive Google Search Console data. Those need a separate check. They are not proven weaknesses.

07 / How to know it worked

MEASURE WHAT
THE BUSINESS GETS.

Use the same clear report across the group, but give each brand the right goals. A dinner booking and a VIP table are not the same result.

01

Dining

Count finished bookings and orders tied to a source when possible. A click on Book is not a confirmed table.

02

Nightlife

Count confirmed tickets, guest-list signups and VIP tables separately. Show which results are requests and which are confirmed.

03

Private events

Request → good fit → quote → booked event. Include time to reply, booked value and why a request did not become an event.

04

Return visits

Count signups with permission, repeat bookings or orders, and people who leave the list. Be clear about results you cannot track.

The actions to track

venue_selectbrand + location
menu_viewmenu + venue + device
booking_startbooking service + ad or post
booking_completeonly when the booking service confirms it
event_inquiry_submita sent request, not just a click
event_bookedevent record + approved booking value

These are suggested tracking names, not tools we found on the sites. Check that results carry across booking services and are not counted twice. Follow consent rules. Keep names, emails and private details out of tracking links.

What we need to check next

  • Agency contract and work log: what the fee covers, what was made, who approved it and who reports results.
  • Ad accounts: spend, goals, locations, ad versions, how often people see them and which results count.
  • Website and search reports: where visitors come from, which pages they use, what they do and how Google finds the site.
  • Booking and order services: correct venue links, finished-booking data and reports we can use.
  • Event request log: real leads, time to reply, fit, booked value and why an event was lost.
  • Social accounts and listings: post results, past content, who owns each page and who answers messages.

Start with read-only access to only what is needed. Approve site changes and data sharing separately.

A useful monthly report

Ask what happened after the click.

Build this report by brand and location. Use actual records. Leave a field blank when it cannot be verified.

Work delivered

What was promised? What posts, ads, photos, videos, pages and reports were delivered? Who approved them? Keep agency fees separate from ad spend.

Money spent

Show ad spend by brand, location and goal. Match platform totals to invoices. Separate production fees, software and media costs.

Guest results

Show useful requests, finished bookings and orders. For MIX, separate free guest list, paid tickets, VIP requests and confirmed tables.

What to change

State what worked, what did not, what is still unknown and the next test. Do not credit an ad for every sale that happened that week.

A few marketing terms, in plain English
Conversion
A useful action, such as a finished booking. A button click is a different action.
Qualified lead
A real request that fits the venue, date, group size and budget well enough to pursue.
Landing page
The first page a guest sees after clicking a post or ad.
Attribution
The rule used to give a post, ad or source credit for a result. It is not proof that the sale would not have happened without it.
ROAS
Sales credited to ads divided by ad spend. It is not profit and does not include every cost.
Baseline
A checked starting point used to compare later results.
Start with real numbers.

First, make sure the numbers are correct. Use a full reporting period as the starting point. Set goals based on seats, staff, margins and current demand. Compare similar weeks and note holidays, launches or closures. A before-and-after chart alone does not prove what caused a change.

LAB SPEED.
REAL WEIGHT.

Lighthouse 12 lab tests on November 6, 2026. Mobile uses Lighthouse’s default slow 4G phone profile. These are controlled lab measurements, not Google real-visitor (CrUX) field data.

SiteMobile scoreMobile LCPDesktop scoreDesktop weightKey bottleneck
Casa Lola4624.5 s5611.4 MB6.5 MB hero video + 2.2 MB skull PNG
Cafeteria 15L5915.8 s774.2 MBHeavy images + render-blocking scripts

How to read thisGoogle’s “good” LCP target is 2.5 seconds or less. Every MAC site missed it in the mobile lab test. Server response was fast (TTFB usually under 100 ms). The weight is the problem. The MAC mobile run also loaded a Cloudflare challenge script (~1.5 MB); real visitors may or may not see that. PageSpeed Insights CrUX field data was unavailable (API quota 429).
What this does not prove

Lab scores are not lost bookings. We did not measure real guest phones or claim Core Web Vitals field failures. Compress video and images first; keep the look.

08 / A clear 90-day plan

FIX. CONNECT.
THEN SCALE.

Three phases. Named owners. A clear way to say each job is done. Agree on scope and staffing after the account review.

01

Fix what gets in the way.

The web, venue and marketing teams agree on what is live, what needs to change and who owns each step.

  • One correct venue listBrand, address, status, hours, phone, menu, booking and event links. Name the person handling Café Ami updates.
  • Fix the proven issuesFix wrong contact links, old dates, policy links, page titles and layout. Open every changed link to check it.
  • Check accounts and trackingGet read-only access, test what is counted, check booking-service limits and list current ads.
  • Set the starting pointDefine a real booking or useful request. List missing data, who replies to guests and what content work is needed.
  • Done when: Priority fixes pass the checklist. Venue details agree. Approved test requests reach the right team. Missing data is clearly listed.

02

Make each next step clear.

Build pages and content around what the guest came to do.

  • Useful page layoutsVenue, menu and event pages that keep the guest’s date and location when a booking service opens.
  • A workable content planA photo and video list for each brand, approved copy, image rights and a clear link for each post.
  • Search and local detailsApproved listing changes, site checks, clear titles and useful event and location pages.
  • Opening and return-visit plansCafé Ami details and optional updates, plus useful follow-up for guests who agree to receive it.
  • Done when: Key tasks work on phones and desktops. Content is approved. Ads reach the right page. Reports count the right results.

03

Keep what works. Learn from the rest.

Marketing and venue teams review results together. Grow the work only when the numbers support it.

  • Small, planned ad testsAgreed goals and budgets, a clear test length, different ad versions and the right location pages.
  • Test easier ways to bookTest the message, button or page order when enough guests visit to learn. Say when a test has no clear answer.
  • Check lead qualityMatch ad requests with real guest needs, staff replies and booked events or orders.
  • A useful monthly reportWhat changed, what it brought in, what is unknown, what to stop and what to fund next.
  • Done when: The team can connect work and spend to useful results, explain missing data and pick the next job without relying on likes alone.

This is a suggested plan, not a price quote or sales forecast. Some work can overlap. Timing depends on access, staff, approvals, consent rules and enough data to learn.

09 / Sources & method

SHOW THE WORK.

You should be able to check our sources, question a finding and turn it into a clear task.

What was reviewed

We checked public MAC and venue websites, actual link targets, desktop screenshots, the event brochure and Instagram posts shown on the sites. We checked Meta’s public Ad Library and Google Ads Transparency, plus Lighthouse 12 lab speed tests. Other sources are named below.

Time: November 6, 2026 UTC. Pages, offers, venues and access can change. We did not send guest forms, make purchases or change any MAC site.

Limits: This is not a full access, security or legal review. Lighthouse 12 lab speed tests were run November 6, 2026; they are not Google CrUX real-user scores. Public Meta and Google ad libraries were checked the same day; they are not private ad-account access. Google Search Console was not reviewed, so we do not claim search rankings.

How to read the labels

Checked Seen on the page, in its code or in a named source.

Access limited We tried the check but could not get a reliable answer.

Proposed A suggested change or test. It is not live and has no promised result.

Priority shows what to address first, not how much money was lost. A link problem’s impact depends on how many guests use it and what happens next.

How we used the evidence

Screenshots keep their original shape and can be enlarged. Some cards also use link or page-code checks. Captions say when that is the case. No screenshot was changed to create a problem. A blocked check is not proof that something is missing. Suggested copy and designs are marked as drafts.

The case for change is simple: fix proven issues, keep details correct and measure what works. It is not a claim that the current agency has wasted money.

Strong venues. Easier choices. Results you can check.
Next: check the accounts, assign the fixes and test the first improved guest path.
